1dd5c036-7a05-5ca4-aae9-1cf585839ebb.title: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity

7b6ba61d-2e00-539a-84d0-84b63bf92be0.title: Identifying Graph Shifts From the First Shifting Theorem

e-21424.problem: Given that $\mathcal{L} \left\{t\sin(\omega t) \right\}=\dfrac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2},$ find the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{-5t}\cdot t\sin(2t)\right\}.$
e-21424.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$
then
$\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{t\sin(2t) \right\} = \frac{2(2)s}{(s^{2}+2^2)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-5t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} & =\frac{2(2)(s+5)}{((s+5)^{2}+{2}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4(s+5)}{((s+5)^{2}+4)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-21590.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity
e-21590.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $g(t) = 2t^2 + 5te^{4t}$ for $s > 4.$
e-21590.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =L{2{t}^{2}+5t{e}^{4t}} \\  & =L{2{t}^{2}}+L{5t{e}^{4t}} \\  & =2L{{t}^{2}}+5L{t{e}^{4t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s > 0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$ then $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{ te^{4t} \right\} = \dfrac{1}{(s-4)^2}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $g(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t)} & =2L{{t}^{2}}+5L{t{e}^{4t}} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+5\cdot \frac{1}{(s-4)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{5}{(s-4)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>4.$

e-21549.knowledge_point: Identifying Graph Shifts From the First Shifting Theorem
e-21549.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
e-21549.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$
then
$\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by $e^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a > 0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a < 0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $6$ units to the left.

e-21531.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s)$ for $s>s_0.$ Suppose we wish to find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-7t} f(t)\}.$ Show the steps to compute this transform.
e-21531.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-7t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-7t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+7)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $\displaystyle F(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t,$ where $s > s_0.$ Therefore, 

$$
\int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s+7)t} \, f(t)\, \textrm{d}t = F(s+7),
$$

where 

$$
s + 7 > s_0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 
s > s_0 - 7.
$$

Question 1
?

Given that L{tcos⁡(ωt)}=s2−ω2(s2+ω2)2, find the Laplace transform L{e4t⋅tcos⁡(3t)}.

a
s2−9((s−4)2+9)2
b
(s−4)2−9(s−4)2+9
c
(s−4)2−4((s−4)2+9)2
d
(s−4)2−9((s−4)2+9)2
e
(s+4)2−9((s+4)2+9)2
Submit

decision.explanation: With ω=3, the given transform is F(s)=(s²−9)/(s²+9)². The first shifting theorem gives L{e^{4t}t cos(3t)}=F(s−4), which is option d.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Given that  $L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}.$
after.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{3}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-{3}^{2}}{((s-4)^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-9}{((s-4)^{2}+9)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Given that  $L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}.$
content.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{3}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-{3}^{2}}{((s-4)^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-9}{((s-4)^{2}+9)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Setting ω=5 gives F(s)=10s/(s²+25)². By the first shifting theorem, multiplication by e^{3t} replaces s with s−3 throughout F(s), giving option e.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Given that $L{t\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{2\omega s}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}.$
after.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}=\frac{2(5)s}{({s}^{2}+{5}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)} & =\frac{2(5)(s-3)}{((s-3)^{2}+{5}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10(s-3)}{((s-3)^{2}+25)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Given that L{tsin⁡(ωt)}=2ωs(s2+ω2)2, find the Laplace transform L{e3t⋅tsin⁡(5t)}.

a
10(s−3)(s−3)2+25
b
10(s+3)((s+3)2+25)2
c
10s((s−3)2+25)2
d
10(s−3)((s−3)2+9)2
e
10(s−3)((s−3)2+25)2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

Using the given result, we have L{tsin⁡(5t)}=2(5)s(s2+52)2.

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get L{e3t⋅tsin⁡(5t)}=2(5)(s−3)((s−3)2+52)2=10(s−3)((s−3)2+25)2.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option e: ω=5 gives 10s/(s²+25)², and multiplication by e^{3t} shifts s to s−3. Option d is incorrect because it uses 9 instead of 5²=25.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem
content.problem: Given that $L{t\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{2\omega s}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}.$
content.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}=\frac{2(5)s}{({s}^{2}+{5}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)} & =\frac{2(5)(s-3)}{((s-3)^{2}+{5}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10(s-3)}{((s-3)^{2}+25)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 3
?

Given that L{cos⁡(ωt)}=ss2+ω2, find the Laplace transform L{e−3t⋅cos⁡(6t)}.

a
s+3(s+3)2+6
b
s(s+3)2+36
c
s−3(s−3)2+36
d
s+3(s−3)2+36
e
s+3(s+3)2+36
Submit

decision.explanation: For ω=6, F(s)=s/(s²+36). The first shifting theorem replaces s with s−(−3)=s+3, giving (s+3)/((s+3)²+36), which is option e.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Given that $L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{-3t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)}.$
after.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{6}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)} & =\frac{s+3}{(s+3)^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{s+3}{(s+3)^{2}+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Given that L{cos⁡(ωt)}=ss2+ω2, find the Laplace transform L{e−3t⋅cos⁡(6t)}.

a
s+3(s+3)2+6
b
s(s+3)2+36
c
s−3(s−3)2+36
d
s+3(s−3)2+36
e
s+3(s+3)2+36
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

Using the given result, we have L{cos⁡(6t)}=ss2+62.

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

L{e−3t⋅cos⁡(6t)}=s+3(s+3)2+62=s+3(s+3)2+36.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem
content.problem: Given that $L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{-3t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)}.$
content.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{6}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)} & =\frac{s+3}{(s+3)^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{s+3}{(s+3)^{2}+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Given that $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{4t}\cdot {t}^{3}}.$
after.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{{t}^{3}}=\frac{3!}{{s}^{4}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}\cdot {t}^{3}} & =\frac{3!}{(s-4)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{(s-4)^{4}}.\end{aligned}

Question 4
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1, find the Laplace transform L{e4t⋅t3}.

a
6(s−4)4
b
6(s+3)4
c
3(s+4)4
d
3(s−4)4
e
6(s−3)4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

Using the given result, we have L{t3}=3!s4.

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

L{e4t⋅t3}=3!(s−4)4=6(s−4)4.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a. Since L{t³}=3!/s⁴=6/s⁴, multiplication by e^{4t} replaces s with s−4, giving 6/(s−4)⁴.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem
content.problem: Given that $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{4t}\cdot {t}^{3}}.$
content.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{{t}^{3}}=\frac{3!}{{s}^{4}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}\cdot {t}^{3}} & =\frac{3!}{(s-4)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{(s-4)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Given that L{tcos⁡(ωt)}=s2−ω2(s2+ω2)2, find the Laplace transform L{e3t⋅tcos⁡(4t)}.

a
(s−3)2−16((s−3)2+16)2
b
(s+3)2−16((s+3)2+16)2
c
(s−3)2−16(s−3)2+16
d
s2−16((s−3)2+16)2
e
(s−3)2−4((s−3)2+16)2
Submit

decision.explanation: With ω=4, F(s)=(s²−16)/(s²+16)². Multiplication by e^{3t} replaces every s with s−3 by the first shifting theorem, giving option a.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Given that $L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}.$
after.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{4}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{4}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)} & =\frac{(s-3)^{2}-{4}^{2}}{((s-3)^{2}+{4}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(s-3)^{2}-16}{((s-3)^{2}+16)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Given that L{tcos⁡(ωt)}=s2−ω2(s2+ω2)2, find the Laplace transform L{e3t⋅tcos⁡(4t)}.

a
(s−3)2−16((s−3)2+16)2
b
(s+3)2−16((s+3)2+16)2
c
(s−3)2−16(s−3)2+16
d
s2−16((s−3)2+16)2
e
(s−3)2−4((s−3)2+16)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

Using the given result, we have L{tcos⁡(4t)}=s2−42(s2+42)2.

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

L{e3t⋅tcos⁡(4t)}=(s−3)2−42((s−3)2+42)2=(s−3)2−16((s−3)2+16)2.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem
content.problem: Given that $L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}.$
content.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{4}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{4}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)} & =\frac{(s-3)^{2}-{4}^{2}}{((s-3)^{2}+{4}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(s-3)^{2}-16}{((s-3)^{2}+16)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: By linearity and shifting, L{5e^{−t}}=5/(s+1) and L{3t³e^{2t}}=3·3!/(s−2)⁴=18/(s−2)⁴. Their sum is option e, valid for s>2.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=5{e}^{-t}+3{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{5{e}^{-t}+3{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} \\  & =L{5{e}^{-t}}+L{3{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} \\  & =5L{{e}^{-t}}+3L{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =5L{{e}^{-t}}+3L{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{s+1}+3\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{5}{s+1}+\frac{18}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =5L{{e}^{-t}}+3L{{t}^{3}{e}^{2t}} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{s+1}+3\cdot \frac{6}{(s-2)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{5}{s+1}+\frac{18}{(s-2)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

decision.explanation: Linearity gives L{f(t)}=L{e^{−2t}}+2L{te^{2t}}. Applying the first shifting theorem to L{1}=1/s and L{t}=1/s² yields 1/(s+2)+2/(s−2)², valid for s>2. This is option d.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+L{2t{e}^{2t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+2L{t{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+2L{t{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

Question 7
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=e−2t+2te2t for s>2.

a
2(s+2)2+1s−2
b
2(s+2)(s−2)2
c
1(s+2)2+2s−2
d
1s+2+2(s−2)2
e
2(s+2)2(s−2)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t+2te2t}=L{e−2t}+L{2te2t}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}

We are given that, for s>0, L{tn}=n!sn+1.

Therefore, we have the following: L{t}=1s2

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a). Therefore, L{te2t}=1(s−2)2.

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}=1s+2+2⋅1(s−2)2=1s+2+2(s−2)2.

This transform is valid for s>2.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d: linearity adds the transforms 1/(s+2) and 2/(s−2)², obtained by shifting L{1}=1/s and L{t}=1/s². The result is valid for s>2.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity
content.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+L{2t{e}^{2t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+2L{t{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t{e}^{2t}} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-2t}}+2L{t{e}^{2t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

Question 8
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=5t2+9te3t for s>3.

a
5s3+9(s−3)2
b
10s2+9(s−3)3
c
10s3+9(s−3)3
d
10s3+3(s−3)2
e
10s3+9(s−3)2
Submit

decision.explanation: By linearity, L{5t²}=5·2!/s³=10/s³. The first shifting theorem gives L{9te^{3t}}=9/(s−3)². Adding gives option e, valid for s>3.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=5{t}^{2}+9t{e}^{3t}$ for $s>3.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{5{t}^{2}+9t{e}^{3t}} \\  & =L{5{t}^{2}}+L{9t{e}^{3t}} \\  & =5L{{t}^{2}}+9L{t{e}^{3t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L{t{e}^{3t}}=\frac{1}{(s-3)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =5L{{t}^{2}}+9L{t{e}^{3t}} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+9\cdot \frac{1}{(s-3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{9}{(s-3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>3.$

Question 8
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=5t2+9te3t for s>3.

a
5s3+9(s−3)2
b
10s2+9(s−3)3
c
10s3+9(s−3)3
d
10s3+3(s−3)2
e
10s3+9(s−3)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

L{f(t)}=L{5t2+9te3t}=L{5t2}+L{9te3t}=5L{t2}+9L{te3t}

We are given that, for s>0, L{tn}=n!sn+1.

Therefore, we have the following: L{t}=1s2L{t2}=2s3

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a). Therefore, L{te3t}=1(s−3)2.

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is

L{f(t)}=5L{t2}+9L{te3t}=5⋅2s3+9⋅1(s−3)2=10s3+9(s−3)2.

This transform is valid for s>3.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity
content.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=5{t}^{2}+9t{e}^{3t}$ for $s>3.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{5{t}^{2}+9t{e}^{3t}} \\  & =L{5{t}^{2}}+L{9t{e}^{3t}} \\  & =5L{{t}^{2}}+9L{t{e}^{3t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}} \\ L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L{t{e}^{3t}}=\frac{1}{(s-3)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =5L{{t}^{2}}+9L{t{e}^{3t}} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+9\cdot \frac{1}{(s-3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{9}{(s-3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>3.$

after.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)=6{e}^{2t}+2{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}$ for $s>2.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{6{e}^{2t}+2{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}} \\  & =L{6{e}^{2t}}+L{2{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}} \\  & =6L{{e}^{2t}}+2L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}} & =\frac{6}{(s+4)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =6L{{e}^{2t}}+2L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-4t}} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{s-2}+2\cdot \frac{6}{(s+4)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{s-2}+\frac{12}{(s+4)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

Question 10
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=e4t+5t3e−t for s>4.

a
1s−4+30(s−1)4
b
1s−4+30(s+1)4
c
1s+4+30(s+1)4
d
1s−4+6(s+1)4
e
4s−4+30(s+1)4
Submit

decision.explanation: By shifting, L{e^{4t}}=1/(s−4) and L{5t³e^{−t}}=5·3!/(s+1)⁴=30/(s+1)⁴. Linearity adds these terms, giving option b, valid for s>4.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{4t}+5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}$ for $s>4.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{4t}+5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{4t}}+L{5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{4t}}+5L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}} & =\frac{6}{(s+1)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{4t}}+5L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4}+5\cdot \frac{6}{(s+1)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{30}{(s+1)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>4.$

Question 10
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=e4t+5t3e−t for s>4.

a
1s−4+30(s−1)4
b
1s−4+30(s+1)4
c
1s+4+30(s+1)4
d
1s−4+6(s+1)4
e
4s−4+30(s+1)4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

L{f(t)}=L{e4t+5t3e−t}=L{e4t}+L{5t3e−t}=L{e4t}+5L{t3e−t}

We are given that, for s>0, L{tn}=n!sn+1.

Therefore, we have the following: L{t3}=6s4

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a). Therefore, L{t3e−t}=6(s+1)4.

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is

L{f(t)}=L{e4t}+5L{t3e−t}=1s−4+5⋅6(s+1)4=1s−4+30(s+1)4.

This transform is valid for s>4.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity
content.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{4t}+5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}$ for $s>4.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{4t}+5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{4t}}+L{5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{4t}}+5L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}} & =\frac{6}{(s+1)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{4t}}+5L{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4}+5\cdot \frac{6}{(s+1)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{30}{(s+1)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>4.$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L{{e}^{3t}f(t)}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
after.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L{{e}^{3t}f(t)},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $3$ units to the right.

after.html:
Question 11
?

Consider a function f(t) for which the Laplace transform is L{f(t)}=F(s). How can we obtain the graph of L{e3tf(t)} from the graph of F(s)?

a
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 3 vertically.
b
Shift the graph of F(s) by 3 units to the left.
c
Shift the graph of F(s) by 3 units to the right.
d
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 3 horizontally.
e
The Laplace transform is unchanged.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

This implies that multiplying a function f(t) by eat shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the s-axis.

  • If a>0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the right.

  • If a<0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of L{e3tf(t)}, we must shift the graph of F(s) by 3 units to the right.

content.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L{{e}^{3t}f(t)}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
content.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L{{e}^{3t}f(t)},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $3$ units to the right.

after.html:
Question 15
?

Consider a function f(t) for which the Laplace transform is L{f(t)}=F(s). How can we obtain the graph of L{e8tf(t)} from the graph of F(s)?

a
Shift the graph of F(s) by 8 units to the left.
b
Shift the graph of F(s) by 8 units to the right.
c
The Laplace transform is unchanged.
d
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 8 vertically.
e
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 8 horizontally.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

This implies that multiplying a function f(t) by eat shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the s-axis.

  • If a>0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the right.

  • If a<0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of L{e8tf(t)}, we must shift the graph of F(s) by 8 units to the right.

decision.explanation: The Laplace kernel is e^{−st}, so the integrand is e^{−st}e^{4t}y(t)=e^{−(s−4)t}y(t). This integral equals Y(s−4) when s−4>s₀, equivalently s>s₀+4.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
Consider a function $y(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{y(t)}=Y(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{4t}y(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}y(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}y(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{4t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-4)t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Y(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-4)t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t=Y(s-4),
$$

where 

$$
s-4>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+4.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Proving the First Shifting Theorem
content.problem:
Consider a function $y(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{y(t)}=Y(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{4t}y(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}y(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}y(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{4t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-4)t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Y(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-4)t}\,y(t)\,\text{d}t=Y(s-4),
$$

where 

$$
s-4>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+4.
$$

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
Consider a function $m(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{m(t)}=M(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-8t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+8)t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $M(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+8)t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t=M(s+8),
$$

where 

$$

content.knowledge_point: Proving the First Shifting Theorem
content.problem:
Consider a function $m(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{m(t)}=M(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-8t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+8)t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $M(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+8)t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t=M(s+8),
$$

where 

$$
s+8>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-8.
$$

Now, recall that $M(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+8)t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t=M(s+8),
$$

where 

$$
s+8>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-8.
$$

decision.explanation: The integrand is e^{−st}e^{2t}f(t)=e^{−(s−2)t}f(t). Its integral equals F(s−2), valid when s−2>s₀, equivalently s>s₀+2.

\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{2t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t=F(s-2),
$$

where 

$$
s-2>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+2.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Proving the First Shifting Theorem
content.problem:
Consider a function $f(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{2t}f(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{2t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t=F(s-2),
$$

where 

$$
s-2>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+2.
$$

\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{2t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-2)t}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t=F(s-2),
$$

where 

$$
s-2>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+2.
$$

decision.explanation: The integrand is e^{−st}e^{−9t}d(t)=e^{−(s+9)t}d(t). Its integral equals D(s+9), valid when s+9>s₀, equivalently s>s₀−9.

$$

$$

Now, recall that $D(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+9)t}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t=D(s+9),

s+9>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-9.

EXPLANATION

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

L{e−9td(t)}=∫0∞e−st⋅e−9td(t)dt=∫0∞e−(s+9)td(t)dt

content.problem:
Consider a function $d(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{d(t)}=D(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{-9t}d(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-9t}d(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-9t}d(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-9t}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+9)t}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $D(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+9)t}\,d(t)\,\text{d}t=D(s+9),
$$

where 

$$
s+9>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-9.
$$

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
Consider a function $g(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{g(t)}=G(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{-3t}g(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}g(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-3t}g(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-3t}\,g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+3)t}\,g(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $G(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,g(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+3)t}\,g(t)\,\text{d}t=G(s+3),
$$

where 

$$
s+3>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-3.
$$

$$

$$
s+3>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-3.
